original_summary: Big Two is a climbing and shedding card game for 2 to 4 players with a 52-card deck. Players beat the previous play with a higher combination of the same kind (single, pair, triple or five-card poker hand) or pass, and the first player to empty their hand wins the deal. Losers are penalised for the cards they still hold.

review.evidence: No simple policy wins. Always passing never sheds a card. Always playing the lowest legal card breaks up pairs and runs and wastes the high cards needed to regain the lead. Always playing the highest card spends 2s early and loses control later. The leader of the first deal is fixed by the cards, but the rotating deal start in multi-deal play evens this out.

Hand-splitting, keeping control cards and card counting all matter, so a better player wins more often. A single deal is still heavily driven by the deal: a hand with four 2s and a straight flush usually wins whatever the opponents do. The original only reduces luck through informal gambling scores over many deals.

Beginners can always play a legal card and shed something. Experts improve through card counting, reading passes as weakness, deciding when to break combinations and timing the last bomb. The game is not solved.
Hands are hidden. Players must infer what opponents hold from what has been played and from their passes, and must plan the order in which they shed their own hand over many tricks.
The winner of a deal is whoever empties their hand first, and penalties are counts of the cards left. Everything is arithmetic, and comparing plays is a ranking lookup.

The game is turn-based and text-only. However, a 52-card deck, 13-card hands, 2 to 4 players and five-card poker hands (straights, flushes, full houses, straight flushes) make the legality checks long, and a deal can run far beyond 40 orbits once it is cut into steps. The gambling scoring is loosely specified ('doubles for many cards left').

problems: P1: Five-card poker hands need long legality and comparison checks (flush, full house, straight flush ordering) that exceed what can be built reliably.
P2: A 52-card deck with 13 to 17 card hands makes each deal too long for a 40-round limit and makes the hidden state large.
P3: A single deal is decided too much by who was dealt the 2s and the bombs, so luck swamps skill.
P4: The scoring is vague ('doubles for many cards left, holding twos, losing on bombs'), so there is no exact arithmetic winner over several deals.
P5: The first leader is the holder of the lowest card, which is random and gives a tempo edge in a one-deal game.
P6: Comparing combinations through suit and rank names needs a lookup table that the engine lacks.

changes.what: Use a 30-card deck numbered 1 to 30. Card number = 3 × (rank − 1) + suit, with ranks 1 to 10 (rank 10 plays the role of the 2s) and suits 1 to 3. Every comparison is then a comparison of numbers.
changes.why: Rank and suit order become plain arithmetic, so no lookup table is needed.

changes.what: Allow only singles, pairs, triples and three-card runs. A triple may also be played as a bomb on any single or pair.
changes.why: This keeps the core tension of Big Two (whether to break a combination, when to bomb) with short legality checks.

changes.what: Play with exactly 3 players, 9 cards each and 3 cards left face-down unseen all deal.
changes.why: Deals are short enough to fit three into 40 orbits. Card counting becomes reasoning under uncertainty rather than exact elimination.

changes.what: Play a match of 3 deals with an exact penalty per deal. The lowest total penalty wins.
changes.why: Averaging over deals and penalising every card left rewards damage control with a weak hand, not only winning with a strong one.

changes.what: The first lead of deal 1 goes to seat A, deal 2 to seat B and deal 3 to seat C, instead of to the holder of the lowest card.
changes.why: Each seat gets the opening tempo exactly once.

changes.what: Add an exact extra penalty for 2s (rank 10) left in hand and double the penalty for a hand of 7 or more cards.
changes.why: This turns the original's gambling flavour into exact arithmetic and punishes hoarding and passivity.

keeps: Hidden hands, with the aim of shedding all your cards first
Climbing play: beat the current combination with the same kind but higher, or pass
Passing does not lock you out of the trick; when everyone else passes, the last player to play clears the pile and leads anything
The highest rank acts as the 2s and suits break ties
Losers penalised by cards left, with extra penalty for unplayed 2s and for big hands

recommendation.reason: The core climbing and shedding game, with its hidden hands and combination planning, fits once the deck and combinations are shrunk. A three-deal penalty match reduces luck.

variation.name: Little Two
variation.summary: A 3-player, 30-card version of Big Two using singles, pairs, triples (which also act as bombs) and three-card runs. It is played as a match of 3 deals, and the lowest total penalty wins.
variation.rules:
CARDS. There are 30 cards numbered 1 to 30. A card's rank is (card + 2) divided by 3, rounded down, giving ranks 1 to 10. Its suit is card − 3 × (rank − 1), giving suits 1 to 3. A higher card number always beats a lower one. Rank 10 (cards 28, 29, 30) are called 'twos'.

SEATS. The players sit as A, B and C. Turn order is always A, then B, then C, then A again.

MATCH. The match has 3 deals and at most 40 orbits. An orbit is one turn for each seat in order.

DEALING. At the start of each deal, shuffle all 30 cards. Deal 9 to each player, privately. Set the remaining 3 cards aside face-down; nobody sees them during the deal. Every player's card count is public at all times.

COMBINATIONS. There are four kinds:
- Single: one card.
- Pair: two cards of the same rank.
- Triple: three cards of the same rank.
- Run: three cards of three consecutive ranks, any suits. Ranks do not wrap around, so 9-10-1 is not a run.
The value of a combination is its highest card number.

THE PILE. The pile holds a current kind and a current value, or is empty.
- When the pile is empty, the player whose turn it is must lead any combination. They may not pass.
- When the pile is not empty, the player whose turn it is may pass, or may play a combination of the same kind with a higher value.
- Bomb: a triple may be played on a single or a pair whatever its value. The pile's kind then becomes triple.
- A triple on the pile can only be beaten by a higher triple.
- A run can only be beaten by a higher run.
Played cards are announced to everyone and removed from the game for the rest of the deal.

PASSING AND CLEARING. A player who passes may play again the next time their turn comes in the same trick. The engine records who made the last play. If play comes back round to that player because both others passed since their play, the pile is cleared and that player must lead.

ILLEGAL PLAYS. An illegal or malformed play counts as a pass. If the player was required to lead, their lowest-numbered card is played as a single instead.

STARTING A DEAL. In deal 1, seat A leads first. In deal 2, seat B leads first. In deal 3, seat C leads first. Seats before the leader in the first orbit of a deal do not act in that orbit.

END OF A DEAL. A deal ends the moment a player plays their last card. That player wins the deal, and the rest of that orbit is skipped. The next deal begins at the start of the next orbit.

PENALTIES. Each non-winner receives a penalty equal to the number of cards left in their hand, plus 1 for each two (rank 10) left in their hand. If they have 7 or more cards left, this penalty is doubled. The deal winner receives 0. Penalties are added to each player's public running total.

END OF THE MATCH. The match ends after the third deal ends, or at the end of orbit 40, whichever comes first. If orbit 40 ends during a deal, that deal is scored as if it had ended with no winner: every player receives a penalty under the rule above.
variation.objective: The player with the lowest total penalty after the match ends wins. If two or three players tie for the lowest total, the match is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Players must plan how to split their 9 cards into combinations. They must decide when to spend twos and triples to take control, and must count cards to infer who holds the remaining twos, given that 3 cards are unseen. Passes reveal weakness, which invites inference about opponents' hands. Three deals with rotating leads, and penalties scaled by cards left, mean a bad hand can still be played well to limit damage, so skill shows across the match. Talk is left out. The interests are directly opposed with a single winner, so the only shared interest is stopping the current leader, and pre-play messages would mostly be unverifiable claims about hands that add words rather than decisions. The reasoning load already sits in card inference and sequencing.

balanced.evidence:
CARD ARITHMETIC CHECK: rank = floor((c+2)/3). Card 1 gives rank 1, card 3 gives rank 1, card 4 gives rank 2 and card 30 gives rank 10. Suit = c - 3(rank-1) gives 1, 2 or 3. So there are 10 ranks of 3 cards, and the three 'twos' are cards 28, 29 and 30. Each player gets 9 cards and 3 are set aside.

PENALTY TABLE (non-winner):
- 1 card left, no twos: 1.
- 3 cards, 1 two: 4.
- 6 cards, 1 two: 7.
- 7 cards, 0 twos: 14 (doubled).
- 8 cards, 2 twos: 20.
- Winner: 0.
The doubling step at 7 cards makes hoarding and stalling costly.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the WINNER RULE (lowest total wins):
(1) Always pass. The player acts only when forced to lead, which happens only after making the last play. That means once at the start of their own deal, after which their lowest single is easily beaten. They finish each deal with about 8 cards, which costs 16 or more after doubling. Against sensible or random opponents, who shed several cards per deal and end at about 0-8, they lose nearly every match.
(2) Always the first or lowest legal option, meaning lead the lowest single and beat with the smallest card. This sheds one card per trick and leaves pairs, triples and runs broken. A sensible player who leads runs and triples sheds 3 cards per lead and keeps the twos and bombs to regain control. The lowest-option player usually ends with 3-6 cards. They beat random play sometimes but lose to sensible play most of the time.
(3) Always the highest or biggest play. This spends the twos and bombs on cheap tricks and loses control later. A sensible player saves the bombs and wins the late tricks.
No policy never loses, and no option is strictly better whatever the opponent does. Passing, beating, splitting and bombing each have counter-situations.

SEATS: the first leader of each deal (A, then B, then C) gets the initiative, and each seat gets it exactly once. There is no information asymmetry, since every hand is private and every count is public. The next leader does not depend on who won the previous deal.

ORBIT-CAP RISK: a typical deal of 5-8 tricks at about 1.5 orbits each, plus skipped partial orbits, takes roughly 9-13 orbits, so about 30-36 for three deals. Deal 3, where C leads, is occasionally cut off. The truncation rule penalises everyone by the same formula, so C loses a little initiative but no seat is structurally favoured.

All three players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS: the rules cover all of the following.
- Each combination kind and its value (the highest card number).
- Which plays beat which: same kind and higher value; a triple bombs a single or a pair; a run is beaten only by a higher run; a triple only by a higher triple.
- Forced leads, and re-entry after a pass.
- Clearing, decided by the recorded last player.
- Illegal plays: they count as a pass, or as the lowest card played as a single when the player must lead.
- The skipped seats before the first leader.
- How a deal ends mid-orbit and when the next deal starts.
- Penalties, including the twos and the doubling.
- Truncation at orbit 40, and ties producing a draw.
I found no situation left unresolved. A player can never be required to lead with 0 cards, because the deal ends at once when someone plays their last card.

FINITE: every trick removes at least 1 card, and the cap of 40 orbits bounds the match.

ARITHMETIC: rank, suit, kind, legality, clearing and penalties are all integer operations on numbers the engine keeps. No judge is needed for the outcome.

LIMITS (each within the platform maximum):
- steps: 14 of 20.
- choice steps: 3 of 4 (one per seat per orbit).
- attributes: 17 of 20. A rough count: 3 hands, 3 totals, 3 counts, pile kind, pile value, last player, deal number, orbit, leader, a deal-over flag and the aside list, which is about 15-17.
- hidden elements: 2 of 3 (the private hands and the aside cards).
- random draws: 1 per round (the shuffle in the deal-start orbit).
- rounds: 40 of 40.
The design uses only supported features: hidden_hands, sequential_choice, fixed_rounds, and a deck handled through list operations. There is no board, clock, trading or binding agreement.

TURN ORDER: the order of play is the point of a climbing game, so sequential turns rather than a simultaneous poll are correct.

TALK: omitting talk for 3 players is sensible. Each player is trying to empty their own hand, with no joint proposal to accept or betray. Talk would mostly add words, and pressure on a near-empty opponent can be inferred from the public counts.

REPEATED-GAME CHECK: there is no cooperate/defect structure, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
SOURCES OF CHANCE: the deal decides who holds the twos and the complete triples (bombs), plus the 3 hidden aside cards. With only 3 deals, variance is meaningful. I estimate chance decides about 40-50% of match results between equal players.

SKILL LEVERS:
(a) Hand partitioning: splitting 9 cards into runs, triples, pairs and singles to minimise the number of tricks needed. Three runs can empty a hand in 3 leads.
(b) Timing control: keeping twos and bombs to regain the lead, and judging when passing is cheaper than beating.
(c) Inference: counting the announced cards over 27 dealt and 3 hidden. This shows which twos and triples are still possible and what an opponent who passed on a pair probably lacks.
(d) Opponent modelling: public card counts show who is close to going out, so a player can block them by leading kinds that player cannot follow, or by bombing.
(e) Penalty management: the threshold at 7 or more cards and the +1 per two give reasons to dump twos or cards when losing the deal is likely.

WHEN ALL PLAY WELL: the deal favours someone each time, but a strong hand can still be blocked. Over 3 deals, with each seat leading once, an inferior hand often avoids the doubled penalty. The winner is not decided by the draw alone. A model that counts cards and partitions its hand clearly beats one that plays greedily (see the balanced evidence).
